title: Structural Hazards: When Two Instructions Want One Unit
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Fixes
quickIdea: A structural hazard is a resource conflict: two instructions in different stages need the same unit in the same cycle and the unit can serve only one. It is a property of the hardware, not of the program's data, and it is fixed by adding hardware or by stalling.
remember: Sarangi's definition 71: a structural hazard is the possibility of instructions not executing because of resource constraints - several instructions wanting one functional unit in one cycle.
The two classic cases: a single memory port wanted by IF and MA in the same cycle, and a functional unit that needs several cycles for some instructions while the stage is designed for one.
Fixes: split instruction and data memories (the Harvard split), duplicate the unit, pipeline the unit internally, or stall one of the two instructions.

A variable-length stage is a structural hazard in time: if an instruction holds EX for c cycles, the instruction behind it loses c - 1 cycles. Total stalls = sum over instruction types of (ceil(t / clock) - 1) x count.

A well-built 5-stage pipeline with separate instruction and data memories and a three-port register file has no structural hazards at all, which is why GATE tests them through multi-cycle functional units instead.

example.prompt: In a pipelined processor the EX stage is a single unit with a 1 ns clock. Of 100 instructions, LOAD takes 1.8 ns in EX (15 of them), IMUL 1.5 ns (10), IDIV 2.5 ns (5), FADD 1.7 ns (10), FSUB 1.7 ns (5), FMUL 2.8 ns (15), FDIV 3.2 ns (5), and the remaining 35 take under 1 ns. How many cycles is the pipeline stalled because of structural hazards in EX?
example.work: Each instruction occupies EX for ceil(t) cycles at a 1 ns clock and delays the next by ceil(t) - 1. LOAD, IMUL, FADD and FSUB take 2 cycles so cost 1 stall each; IDIV and FMUL take 3 so cost 2 each; FDIV takes 4 so costs 3. The total is 15 + 10 + 2x5 + 10 + 5 + 2x15 + 3x5 = 15 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 30 + 15 = 95.
example.answer: 95 stall cycles, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.60.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.60 is the pure structural-hazard question: a multi-cycle EX unit, a table of instruction types, and a request for the number of stalled cycles. GATE CSE 2018 Q.50 is the same idea with the stage occupancy given directly instead of the time, and its 115 extra cycles are the same arithmetic.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: In the 2026 Set 1 table, the EX stage is replaced by a pipelined unit that accepts a new instruction every cycle. What becomes of the 95 stall cycles?
variations.why: It shows that the hazard was a property of the unit, not of the instruction mix, and that the fix is hardware.
variations.answer: They fall to zero: a pipelined multiplier or divider keeps the stage busy internally and lets a new instruction enter each cycle. The latency of an FDIV is unchanged at 3.2 ns, but it no longer blocks the stage, so the 95 cycles of throughput are recovered without changing any instruction.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a single memory port create a structural hazard in a 5-stage pipeline, and what removes it?
variations.why: It is the textbook case and the one students mislabel as a data hazard.
variations.answer: Because IF reads an instruction every cycle while MA reads or writes data, and in the steady state both want memory in the same cycle. Separate instruction and data caches or memories remove the conflict; a single unified cache would need a stall every time an instruction fetch and a data access coincide.

trap.what: Counting ceil(t) cycles per instruction as the stall instead of ceil(t) - 1.
trap.why: The instruction occupies the stage for ceil(t) cycles, but only the cycles beyond the first are lost to the pipeline, because the first cycle is the one the stage was going to be busy with anyway.
trap.counterexample: 2026 Set 1 Q.60: using the occupancies 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3 and 4 gives 15x2 + 10x2 + 5x3 + 10x2 + 5x2 + 15x3 + 5x4 = 160, against the accepted 95. The overcount is 65, exactly the number of instructions in the program that need more than one cycle in EX.

check.question: In a 40-instruction program the EX unit takes 2 cycles for 10 instructions and 1 cycle for the rest. How many stall cycles does EX cause?
check.answer: 10 cycles: each of the 10 long instructions costs one extra cycle.
check.explanation: ceil(2) - 1 = 1 per long instruction, and the other 30 take one cycle so cost nothing.
